Abstract: And with two opposing operational constraints in production scenarios, contemporary pipelines are bound to encounter a nearly insurmountable cognitive friction. First, static application security testing (SAST) has a false positive rate of greater than 70% reported, and generative massive language models produce syntactically valid yet semantically invalid patches that break contracts and introduce secondary vulnerabilities. To address the systemic architectural vulnerabilities within all three paradigms, this paper introduces Aegis One AI - an end-to-end closed-loop Dev Sec Ops adversarial defense copilot. Aegis One AI builds static analysis and autonomous repair via four orthogonal pillars: (a) an authorized Pre-Flight Scope Guard that guarantees deterministic perimetric boundaries, (b) an efficient hybrid detection engine that hybridizes AST static taint tracking and dynamic fuzzing telemetry, (c) a heterogeneous Security Knowledge Graph that couples source code AST sinks, HTTP routes, and database entities to produce an explainable 6-factor composite risk priority, and (d) a containerized 4-stage disposable Docker sandbox which enforces contract-preserving validation with automatic state rollback upon regression, while cryptographically chaining all security operations, patch syntheses and validation decisions onto a tamper-evident SHA-256 Merkle audit trail with Ed25519 digital signature signing. Empirical evaluation over a benchmark suite of 120 synthetic and enterprise-grade web vulnerability scenarios shows Aegis One AI achieves 94.6% precision, 92.8% recall, 91.5% semantic patch validity, and 98.4% automated deployment with no regressions.
Intro_1: Modern web application architectures are evolving quickly with promising components for the future including high-performance-pipeline CI/CD workloads. Initial research indicates that while Agile processes can help both accelerate feature delivery and increase an organization's attack surface, traditional Static Application Security Testing is typically based on heuristics grounded in syntax that is likely to generate high rates of alert fatigue where possibly 75% of these findings are false positives. Dynamic Application Security Testing can only hope to ultimately detect exploitability during runtime without any guarantee of sufficient code coverage or structural perspective on server-side execution.
Intro_2: That said, recent successes of LLMs for code synthesis have also sparked immense interest in Automated Program Repair. Just deploying raw generative LLMs in a mission-critical security toolkit can be disastrous. In practice, foundation models often synthesize code that "looks right", but, in reality, may be semantically insecure, introducing "regressions" or subtly altering business invariants. Existing APR frameworks have no theoretical basis; they do not formally verify whether a code change breaks any runtime contract, alters architecture semantics, or opens a new attack vector.
Intro_3: This paper presents Aegis One AI, an autonomous, closed-loop Dev Sec Ops security copilot that mitigates these basic constraints by closing the gap between static vulnerability discovery and verified programmatic repair. Aegis One AI offers a new paradigm based on combining multi-modal application inspection with mathematically bounded patch verification (i.e. Enabling each repair to be predicted as safe, context-aware and contract-preserving).
Threat_Model: This scenario assumes an external attacker on the public Internet and an authenticated malicious insider with application credentials with low value and insignificant on-path value. The attacker would attempt to exploit common web application weaknesses, including Structured Query Language Injection, Cross-Site Scripting, Broken Object-Level Authorization, and Server-Side Request Forgery. It also assumes a non-trusted generative model that produces stochastic outputs with the potential to hallucinate, logically fail, or include backdoors. Prior to any dynamic analysis or mutation of code, Aegis One AI has to satisfy a specification that is explicitly authorized. Any probing attempt that does not follow this specification will be rejected at ingress with a 403 HTTP Forbidden status and will not probe production or third-party cloud infrastructure by mistake.
Hybrid_Detection: Most "analyzers" work in isolation, leading to high false positives and some code paths being ignored. Aegis One AI combines both static and dynamic approaches into a single dual-engine pipeline. Aegis One AI extracts target route handler parameters, URL args, and data types from the AST traversal of the Semgrep target, turning the static AST based discovery into dynamic fuzzing hypothesis, and then the dynamic fuzzing harness uses an embedded OWASP ZAP API controller to verify the hypothesis generated from the AST. Further to differentiate true code execution reflection from function title, the Aegis One AI injects cryptographic canary strings. Where the execution shows the canary in the response body without sanitization, or response latency exceeds 3.0s under time-delay injection, then the dynamic harness is likely to produce exploitability.
Knowledge_Graph: Isolated vulnerability scanners treat each vulnerability as a point detection ignoring the topology of the system where the component resides. A SQL injection on a public metrics analytics route handled by a remote admin analytics route would have very different enterprise risk of a payload embedded in a payment processing microservice that stores personally identifiable information in plaintext. Aegis One AI ingests a cross-domain heterogeneous directed Security Knowledge Graph, modeled using Neo4j and NetworkX. It models code sinks, code routes, and database schemas and PII sensitivity, with 890 nodes and 1,420 edges, employing personalized Page Rank centrality and shortest-path taint flow to derive an interpretable six-factor composite vulnerability score.
Patch_Synthesis: Forgo on unrestricted prompts or general-purpose language models. Instead, Aegis One AI infuses its untrusted generative repair via a constrained, grammar-guided program patching module built on the foundation of its AST. Once an AST sink node that maintains a verified vulnerability is identified, our patch synthesizer harnesses a more localized backward program slice containing only the relevant dataflow dependencies. As per the research works, the output of unconstrained language models might have highly unstable refactoring behaviors that are crafted by removing necessary business logic, removing authorization checks, or replacing native classes with rough comments. In addition, Aegis One AI employs deterministic programmatic Refusal Guards to verify the patch diffs prior to running. If any refusal rule is invoked, the output patch is instantly rejected, and the prompt engine will be more likely to re-synthesize with a transparent violation penalty.
Sandbox_Validation: To prevent an automated security patch from disrupting production workloads, Aegis One AI deploys an isolated validation pipeline, built around disposable Docker containers. Each patch candidate is tested in a temporary container, spawned from the target application's pristine base image. The container environment is defined by mandatory cgroups v2 resource quotas, capability dropping, and ephemeral bridge networking isolated from the host. The sandbox runs through four phases: Stage 1 (Clean Baseline Verification); Stage 2 (Patch Application and AST Integrity); Stage 3 (Dynamic Vulnerability Elimination), and Stage 4 (Functional Regression Testing). If the patch fails at any phase, the automated rollback mechanism will likely return the workspace to the pristine base image, log telemetry on the failure, and inform the developer console of the regression.
Merkle_Audit: In a regulated enterprise context, the outcome of any automated change must be mathematically non-repudiable. Aegis One AI utilizes an append-only cryptography log chain with SHA-256. To provide author non-repudiation to the distributed CI/CD runners, the block header is signed with an Ed25519 private key. Any backdating of the previous log record is thought to cause the mathematical invariant to break, which would alarm security auditors.
Results_Ablation: The empirical evaluation on the suite of benchmark, 120 enterprise and synthetic web vulnerability scenarios suggests, Aegis One AI will have a 94.6% precision, 92.8% recall, 93.7% F1 score, 91.5% semantic patch validity and 98.4% zero regression automated deployment rate. The static-only scanner has higher false-positive rate, while the dynamic-only scanner demonstrates high precision but misses the unexercised route. By cross-validation of AST taint hypothesis with dynamic canary fuzzing, Aegis One AI can demonstrate a 15.8% F1 score improvement over static-only scanning; it is likely that disabling dynamic canary fuzzing engine will lower the precision to 78.4% and removing Security Knowledge Graph may lower the recall to 84.5%; lastly, removing the container sandbox verification will likely lower the zero regression deployment rate to 61.2% and demonstrates the need for isolated runtime testing and automated rollback to prevent broken code from being introduced into production.
Discussion_Declarations: Such overhead is shown to have consistently measured an average turnaround latency of 34.2 seconds/patch with container hypervisors on web applications. However, web applications requiring multi-factor authentication sequences pose a challenge as they require recorded session macros to be used by the dynamic fuzzer to deep-nest views prior to enumeration. Future work involves the optimisation of verification latency using hardware-accelerated microVM sandboxing techniques to achieve sub-second performance. Furthermore, the full software source code, along with experimental evaluation benchmarks, containerized vulnerable lab targets and scripts to reproduce the entire experiment for Aegis One AI are available at https://github.com/Praveen Kanth-N/Aegis One-AI, released under the open source MIT License for full academic reproducibility.
